strengths: Addresses two genuinely under-explored perceptual criteria in UV parameterization—semantic coherence and seam visibility—that prior automatic methods largely ignore, and combines them within a single differentiable framework.

The technical pipeline is coherent and well described: a bi-directional cycle-mapping backbone for geometry-preserving parameterization, a ShDF+graph-cut based semantic partitioning scheme, a differentiable soft seam-extraction procedure, and an ambient-occlusion-weighted seam loss that is fully justified and mathematically detailed.

Reasonably thorough qualitative results across a variety of meshes (simple primitives to more complex articulated/mechanical objects), and clear visual evidence (checkerboard texturing, AO histograms) that the visibility-aware objective shifts seams toward occluded regions.

Useful ablations isolating the effect of the partitioning strategy (ShDF vs. SAMesh) and of the semantic/visibility losses on geometric distortion metrics, showing the added objectives do not substantially harm conformality/equiareality.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendix on the ShDF partitioning algorithm, network architecture (layer-wise Table 3), and loss formulations.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is conducted on only a handful of individual meshes (Rabbit, Cow, Fish, Duckie, etc.) rather than a larger benchmark dataset (e.g., ShapeNet, Thingi10k, ABC), making it unclear how well the reported metrics generalize and whether differences are statistically meaningful (no variance/error bars reported).

The semantic-awareness quantitative metric (Hamming distance/Rand Index) uses SAMesh output as a pseudo-ground-truth, which is questionable since SAMesh is itself an unsupervised heuristic segmentation baseline also used elsewhere in the paper (including in the ablation as an alternative partitioner)—this creates a somewhat circular evaluation without true semantic ground truth or human annotation.

The visibility metric (mean seam AO) is essentially the same quantity the visibility loss directly optimizes, so strong performance on this metric is close to tautological; a more convincing evaluation would use an independent rendering-based seam-artifact measure across multiple lighting/viewpoints or a human perceptual study, which is absent.

No comparison against several directly relevant semantic-aware or visibility-aware baselines explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., Vermandere et al. 2024, Mukherjee et al. 2024, Seamster, GraphSeam, Weill-Duflos et al. 2023)—comparisons are limited mostly to FlexPara, OptCuts, and generic industry tools.

The method appears to require per-mesh (test-time) optimization of the backbone and per-part networks (Algorithm 1 shows a training loop per mesh), which is in tension with the title's framing as "representation learning"; scalability/generalization to unseen shapes without retraining and total end-to-end optimization cost per mesh are not clearly discussed.

Limited discussion of failure cases, computational cost/scalability trade-offs of the per-part partition-and-parameterize approach (including UV-space utilization losses from the simple grid-based atlas packer), and sensitivity to hyperparameters (K, τ_scale, β, γ, λ_vis) is largely absent from the main text.

strengths: The paper tackles a practical and underexplored problem—automating UV parameterization with both semantic and visibility awareness—that is well-motivated by real content-creation pipelines.

The overall pipeline is clearly described, with a well-organized architecture (deform/wrap/cut/unwrap bi-directional cycle backbone), differentiable AO-weighted seam loss, and a partition-and-parameterize strategy for semantic charting.

The paper includes fairly extensive qualitative figures (main paper + appendix) across multiple mesh categories and viewpoints, plus ablations isolating the semantic-partitioning choice (ShDF vs. SAMesh) and the visibility loss.
Reasonable engineering detail and formulas are provided (losses, AO computation, seam extraction), which aids conceptual reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation of 'semantic awareness' is circular: Hamming distance/Rand Index are computed against SAMesh outputs used as a pseudo ground truth, yet SAMesh is also presented as an alternative/competing partitioner in the ablations—this undermines the validity of the main quantitative semantic-awareness metric.

The paper explicitly identifies Vermandere et al. (2024) and Mukherjee et al. (2024) as the only prior works on semantic-aware UV mapping, and Weill-Duflos et al. (2023)/Ray et al. (2010) as prior visibility-aware seam placement work, yet none of these are included as experimental baselines; comparisons are instead limited to generic geometry-focused tools (Maya, Blender SmartUV, xatlas) and a geometry-only backbone (FlexPara) and classic OptCuts, which were not designed for these objectives, making the comparisons somewhat of a strawman.

No human perceptual/user study is conducted despite the paper's central claims being about perceptual criteria (reduced visible seam artifacts, semantically coherent charts); the visibility claim is validated only via the same AO proxy that is directly optimized during training, which is close to tautological (the loss directly minimizes seam AO, and the metric then shows seam AO is lower).

'Semantic awareness' as implemented is purely a classical geometric heuristic (Shape Diameter Function + graph cuts, from 2008), not a learned or semantically grounded signal (e.g., no text/image/label supervision); conflating geometric-thickness partitioning with true semantic part awareness is a notable overclaim relative to the title and framing as 'semantic objectives.'

The method is a per-mesh/per-shape optimization procedure (Algorithm 1 trains network weights per input mesh via iterative gradient descent), not a generalizable trained representation that amortizes across meshes; describing this as 'unsupervised representation learning' is somewhat misleading, and no train/inference time breakdown or generalization experiment across unseen shapes is reported.

The evaluation set is small and consists mostly of simple, smooth toy meshes (bunny, cow, duck, fish, torus, vase); the one experiment on 'complex' meshes (Fig. 12) shows visibly noisy, fragmented UV atlases, raising scalability/robustness concerns that are not discussed or quantified.

No end-to-end demonstration of the stated downstream motivation (texture generation/synthesis quality) is provided—only a simple checkerboard-pattern sanity check is used instead of actual generative texturing pipelines, which weakens the paper's core claimed significance.

Ablations show the visibility-aware loss noticeably degrades equiareality (0.6707 to 0.6093 in Table 5), which is downplayed as 'minor' without statistical justification or deeper analysis of the geometry-quality/visibility trade-off.
No variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for any quantitative results, and some metric tables are visually hard to parse/verify, limiting confidence in the reported improvements.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: jointly modeling semantic-awareness and visibility-awareness in automatic UV parameterization, going beyond the purely geometric objectives (distortion, bijectivity) used by most prior learning-based methods.

The overall framework is well-motivated and clearly decomposed into interpretable stages (bi-directional cycle mapping backbone, ShDF-based semantic partitioning, AO-based differentiable seam/visibility loss), with reasonably detailed methodology and appendix documentation (e.g., ShDF computation, loss definitions, network architecture) that aids reproducibility.
The differentiable soft seam-extraction and AO-weighted seam loss (Eq. 5-7) is a clean, technically sound way to make seam placement end-to-end trainable without heuristic cut selection.

Ablations (ShDF vs. SAMesh partitioner, with/without visibility loss) support the claim that adding semantic/visibility objectives does not significantly harm core geometric metrics (conformality, equiareality), and qualitative seam-AO histograms (Fig. 6, 7) plausibly show seams shifted toward occluded regions.
Code is stated to be publicly released, and the paper compares against both learning-based (FlexPara, OptCuts) and industry-standard (Maya, Blender, xatlas) baselines.
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is quite limited: quantitative tables (Table 1, 2) are computed on an unspecified/small "collection of representative meshes" without reporting the number of test shapes, per-shape variance, or statistical significance, weakening confidence that reported gains generalize beyond the handful of visualized examples.

The semantic-awareness metric (Hamming distance / Rand Index) is computed against SAMesh outputs used as a pseudo-ground-truth, yet SAMesh is simultaneously used as an alternative partitioner in the ablation; this creates a circular evaluation and makes it hard to assess true semantic-alignment quality independent of the chosen reference segmenter.

Although the paper explicitly reviews semantic-aware (Vermandere et al. 2024; Mukherjee et al. 2024) and visibility-aware (Weill-Duflos et al. 2023; Ray et al. 2010; Sheffer & Hart 2002) prior work as the closest related methods, none of these specialized baselines are included in the quantitative or qualitative comparisons—only general-purpose parameterization tools (FlexPara, OptCuts, Maya, Blender, xatlas) are benchmarked, leaving the central claim of outperforming prior semantic/visibility-aware approaches largely unverified.

The core perceptual claim (reduced perceptible seam artifacts) is only supported by an ambient-occlusion proxy and visual checkerboard insets; no human/user study is conducted to validate that the proposed seams are actually perceived as less visible, despite visibility being framed as a perceptual criterion throughout.

The UV atlas aggregation/packing step is admittedly a simple, deterministic uniform grid packer; its impact on texel density/distortion trade-offs versus more advanced production packers is not quantitatively examined.

The method builds heavily on the existing FlexPara bi-directional cycle-mapping backbone (reused largely as-is per Appendix A.2), somewhat limiting the technical novelty to the added semantic-partition-and-parameterize pipeline and the AO-weighted seam loss; the incremental nature relative to FlexPara could be made more explicit.

No discussion of failure cases, robustness to noisy/non-manifold meshes, sensitivity to the number of semantic parts K (which appears to require manual specification), or computational/training cost at scale (e.g., very high-poly meshes), limiting the practical assessment of generality.

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical bottleneck (manual UV parameterization) with a well-motivated combination of two under-explored perceptual objectives: semantic alignment and visibility-aware seam placement.

The overall pipeline is unsupervised and differentiable, built on an existing geometry-preserving backbone, with clear per-module loss design (semantic partition + per-part parameterization + atlas packing; AO-weighted differentiable seam detection).

Extensive empirical evaluation: qualitative comparisons across multiple meshes/viewpoints, quantitative metrics (Hamming distance, Rand Index, mean seam AO, conformality, equiareality), and a fairly large user study (115 participants split into expert/general groups) showing strong preference for the proposed method.

Thorough ablation studies (segmentation backbone choice: ShDF vs. SAMesh vs. PartField; UV packing strategies; visibility loss on/off; combined vs. individual objective pipelines) and an honest discussion of trade-offs between geometry-preservation and semantic/visibility objectives.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendix with architecture/layer tables, algorithmic pseudocode, loss definitions, and transparent disclosure of LLM usage for writing.
weaknesses: The two most directly related prior works explicitly cited as tackling the same problems individually (Vermandere et al. 2024 for semantic-aware UV mapping, Weill-Duflos et al. 2023 / Sheffer & Hart 2002 / Ray et al. 2010 for visibility/seam-aware placement) are never used as empirical baselines; comparisons are instead limited to generic parameterization tools (FlexPara, OptCuts, Maya, Blender, xatlas) that do not target these objectives, making the central novelty claim ("first to jointly address both") harder to substantiate quantitatively against the closest competitors.

The core geometry-preserving backbone is explicitly non-novel (reused from Zhao et al. 2025/FlexPara); the semantic partitioning relies on a classical hand-crafted algorithm (Shapira et al. 2008 ShDF + GMM + graph cuts) rather than a learned method, so the technical novelty is largely confined to the loss formulations that connect these existing components, which is a comparatively incremental contribution.

The visibility-aware pipeline incurs a drastic training-time overhead (roughly 20-30x slower than the FlexPara baseline per Table 9), with only speculative future-work mitigations (parallelization, spatial hashing) proposed rather than demonstrated, raising practical scalability concerns.

Method requires per-mesh optimization (no amortized/generalizable model), and all demonstrated meshes are small-to-moderate single objects (rabbit, cow, duckie, etc.) rather than a standard large-scale 3D benchmark (e.g., ShapeNet/Objaverse), limiting evidence of generality and production-scale applicability.

The semantic-awareness quantitative metric (Hamming distance/Rand Index) uses SAMesh outputs as a proxy "ground truth," which is itself an automatic, imperfect segmentation method, raising concerns about circularity/validity of this evaluation.

Reported gains are occasionally marginal or come with trade-offs (e.g., Table 7 shows only slight conformality improvements and reduced equiareality for the combined pipeline; Table 3 Hamming distance improvement over baselines is moderate), while user-study preference numbers are extremely lopsided (e.g., 91-93% preference) without reported inter-rater agreement or statistical significance testing, which could reflect an easy/binary comparison design rather than robust superiority.

The ablation on segmentation strategy (Table 6, Figs. 14-15) shows PartField often producing qualitatively better semantic segmentations than the adopted default (ShDF), and the paper acknowledges no clear causal link between segmentation quality and final UV geometry metrics, somewhat undermining confidence in the specific design choice used for the main results.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: jointly optimizing semantic-awareness and visibility-awareness in automatic UV parameterization, which is a genuine pain point in 3D content pipelines.

The paper is thorough in presenting qualitative and quantitative evaluation, including a fairly large (115-participant) user study split into expert and general groups, and extensive ablations (partitioning strategy, UV packing strategy, loss ablations) in the appendix.
Reasonable set of baselines for comparison (FlexPara, OptCuts, Maya, Blender, xatlas), covering both commercial and research tools.

Clear exposition of the pipeline (3D semantic partitioning via ShDF, per-part parameterization, atlas aggregation; AO-based differentiable seam-visibility loss) with detailed appendix formulas and algorithm box.
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: the paper explicitly states it does not contribute a new parameterization backbone (reuses the bi-directional cycle mapping network from Zhao et al., 2025); the main contributions are a segmentation-then-parameterize engineering pipeline and an AO-based soft seam loss, both built from well-known components (Shape Diameter Function, ambient occlusion as visibility proxy, soft seam detection via neighbor-distance thresholds). The combination is useful but incremental rather than conceptually novel.

Evaluation is conducted on a very small number of meshes (roughly a dozen shapes such as rabbit, cow, fish, duckie, potion, flip-flop, spot, squidward house, elephant, etc.), with no large-scale quantitative benchmark across hundreds/thousands of shapes; this raises concerns about generalizability of the reported gains.

The semantic-awareness quantitative metric (Hamming distance / Rand Index) uses SAMesh outputs as a pseudo-ground-truth reference, which is methodologically questionable since SAMesh is itself one of the compared/alternative partitioners elsewhere in the paper (potential circularity/bias in favor of methods that resemble SAMesh-like segmentations).

Substantial, largely unaddressed computational overhead: the visibility-aware pipeline's training time is reported as ~20-30x slower than the FlexPara baseline (Table 9, e.g., ~31,160s vs ~1,285s average), and the semantic-aware pipeline's inference time is also notably higher due to per-part processing; the paper only offers these as "future work" mitigations (multi-threading, spatial hashing) without actually implementing or validating them.

The user study, while large, lacks methodological detail on blinding/randomization of method order and the lopsided preference percentages (often >90% for the proposed method) raise concern about potential study design bias; no inter-rater reliability or statistical significance testing is reported.

The geometry-preservation trade-off is non-trivial: the semantic/visibility-aware objectives noticeably degrade distortion metrics in some settings (e.g., larger equiareality drop for the visibility-aware pipeline in Table 7), and this trade-off is only partially mitigated by the combined pipeline, suggesting the perceptual gains come at real cost to standard parameterization quality.

The atlas aggregator/packer described in Sec. 3.4 is intentionally simplistic (grid-based, fixed-size cells), which likely under-utilizes UV space and texel density compared to advanced commercial packers (acknowledged by the authors' own ablation showing commercial tools achieve higher texel density/utilization), undermining the practicality of the proposed pipeline as a drop-in replacement for production use.

Ablations on partitioning strategy (ShDF vs. SAMesh vs. PartField) show inconsistent, non-causal relationships between segmentation quality and downstream geometric metrics, and the paper itself admits "no obvious or general relationship," weakening the justification for ShDF as the chosen partitioner.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important gap: UV parameterization methods that are both semantically coherent and visibility-aware, which prior work has only tackled individually.

The differentiable soft-seam-detection + AO-weighted seam loss (Eqs. 5-7) is a clean, technically sound way to make seam placement differentiable and bias cuts toward occluded regions; qualitative (Figs. 4, 9-11) and quantitative (seam-AO histograms, Fig. 8) evidence consistently supports the claim.

Extensive ablation studies: partitioner choice (ShDF vs. SAMesh vs. PartField), atlas packing strategy vs. commercial tools, visibility loss on/off, and geometry-preservation vs. semantic/visibility trade-off (Table 7) — these give good insight into design choices and their costs.

User study with both expert (45, industry UV/layout/modeling artists) and general (70) participants, with strong and consistent preference for the proposed method across both groups, lending some empirical weight to the perceptual claims.

Transparent reporting of limitations, including training/inference time overhead (Tables 8-9) and the geometry-distortion trade-off incurred by adding semantic/visibility objectives (Table 7), rather than hiding them.
Reasonably thorough related-work positioning and reuse of an established low-distortion backbone (FlexPara) is explicitly acknowledged rather than mis-claimed as novel.
weaknesses: Core novelty is somewhat incremental: the low-distortion mapping backbone is directly adopted from FlexPara (Zhao et al. 2025) unmodified; the paper's contribution is largely a combination of known components (ShDF segmentation, AO-as-visibility-proxy, soft/differentiable seam detection) into a pipeline rather than a fundamentally new parameterization technique.

Semantic-aware and visibility-aware objectives are mostly presented and evaluated as two separate pipelines (Sec. 3.3 vs 3.4, Table 1 vs Table 3) rather than a single jointly-trained framework as the abstract implies; the combined "Visibility+Semantic-Aware" variant only appears in one ablation table (Table 7), which weakens the claimed unification.

The semantic-awareness quantitative metric (Hamming distance/Rand Index) is computed against SAMesh outputs as a pseudo-ground-truth, which is itself an automatic unsupervised segmentation method rather than true annotated ground truth — this is methodologically circular and undermines the validity of the semantic-awareness numbers.

The user study's forced-choice questions (Fig. 16) directly ask participants to judge seam visibility/semantic alignment, which is exactly what the method is optimized for, making near-unanimous preference (often >90%) somewhat expected/circular rather than strong independent validation; no information is given about potential author/organizational ties to the expert participant pool.

No direct comparison to the specific semantic-aware (Vermandere et al. 2024; Mukherjee et al. 2024) or visibility-aware (Weill-Duflos et al. 2023; Ray et al. 2010) prior works that the paper explicitly cites as the only existing work addressing these objectives individually — comparisons are limited to geometry-focused baselines (FlexPara, OptCuts, Maya, Blender, xatlas).

The visibility-aware pipeline incurs very large training overhead (up to ~28x slower than FlexPara per Table 9), which is a substantial practical limitation only discussed deep in the appendix rather than foregrounded as a key limitation.

Quantitative evaluation is conducted on a small number of meshes (handful of shapes per table: rabbit, cow, fish, duckie, etc.); no large-scale/category-diverse benchmark is used, so generalization across more complex or diverse mesh categories (e.g., Fig. 13 examples) is only shown qualitatively without numbers.

The default atlas-packing strategy (simple deterministic equal-size grid) is acknowledged to be suboptimal relative to commercial packers (Table 5/Fig. 7 ablation), yet texel-density/UV-space-utilization is not reported for the main comparisons in Tables 1 and 3, leaving open whether reported distortion/visibility gains come at the cost of poor UV-space efficiency relative to baselines.
